name: AEWA World Heavyweight Championship of the World
notes: Six lineage changes traced through 1997 from the fed's own broadcasts and newsletters; the top belt of the promotion, defended on both of its 1997 pay-per-views.
epitaph: The AEWA's own top belt changed hands six times in 1997 alone. Shane Matthews carried it into the year off a battle-royal win the previous November, lost it to Deranged on a chair shot in January, and watched Deranged lose it to "Crimson" Joe Reed at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. Reed's first reign lasted less than two months: Heavy Metal took it off him in a four-way at AEWA Extreme in April, and was himself dethroned within weeks by "Superman" Mike Stewart in a match the AEWA's own record does not carry at all — it survives only as footage replayed on a rival federation's pay-per-view. Reed took the belt back from Stewart at Battle Klash II that summer, in a show that briefly made him champion of two federations at once, and was still champion in the fed's own newsletter as late as 30 November 1997. A rival's own Top 200 write-up records that Randall Osbourne finally ended that reign sometime in 1998, past the edge of the wing's own 1997 record.

name: AEWA North American Championship
notes: Four lineage changes traced through 1997, ending the corpus's own coverage vacant with a tournament under way.
epitaph: A mid-card belt that moved constantly and then simply stopped: Justin Trouble held it into 1997, lost it to Deathwatch in a triangle match at the promotion's own Kickoff '97, saw the Caretaker take it at AEWA Extreme in April, and won it back himself by the end of August. By the fed's own 2 October newsletter the title is vacant, with a tournament already under way to fill it — the last word this corpus has on the belt.

name: AEWA Television Championship
notes: One lineage change traced through 1997, both reigns defended repeatedly including a steel-cage defense at the promotion's own AEWA Extreme.
epitaph: Sir Gallade carried this belt into 1997 off a December 1996 win over Randall Osbourne and held it through both of the fed's own 1997 pay-per-views, including a steel-cage defense against Osbourne at AEWA Extreme. By the end of August "Bullywug" Glenn Hudson had taken it from him, and Hudson was still defending it as the corpus's own coverage closes out in early October.

name: AEWA Light Heavyweight Championship
notes: Four lineage changes traced through 1997; the belt's own history runs through the AEWA's wholly-owned regional promotion as well as its own flagship shows.
epitaph: Penance opened 1997 as champion, defending against Adam Anderson in January before losing the belt to the Holy Ghost on Saturday Night Slam later that same month. "Cardiac Kid" Joey Valachi took it from the Holy Ghost at the promotion's own Kickoff '97, announced as the show's own mystery challenger, and carried it into the AEWA's regional promotion, where he defended it to a time-limit draw against the regional promotion's own Marc Thomas. By the fed's own 2 October newsletter, Fuse is champion, having already defended the belt against Valachi in September.

name: AEWA World Tag Team Championship
notes: Retired into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship on 16 April 1997.
epitaph: The Machines held this belt into 1997 and defended it against the West Coast Connection at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. It stopped existing as its own belt on 16 April 1997, at AEWA Extreme, when the Machines beat the National Tag Team champions, the Assassins, in a dedicated unification match and the two lineages became one — the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship.

name: AEWA National Tag Team Championship
notes: Retired into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship on 16 April 1997.
epitaph: Graphic Violence held this belt into 1997 before losing it to the Assassins at the promotion's own Kickoff '97. It stopped existing as its own belt on 16 April 1997, at AEWA Extreme, when the Assassins lost a dedicated unification match to the World Tag Team champions, the Machines, merging the two lineages into the AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship.

name: AEWA Unified World Tag Team Championship
notes: Created 16 April 1997 at AEWA Extreme, merging the World and National Tag Team lineages in a dedicated unification match — the single cleanest structural fact in the wing's own dossier.
epitaph: Born at AEWA Extreme on 16 April 1997, when the Machines beat the Assassins in a match built specifically to merge the fed's own World and National tag lineages into one belt: the referee hands over "the new Unified Tag Team Title belts" and the ring announcer crowns the Machines the first Unified champions on the spot. By the end of August the West Coast Connection held it, and were still defending it in late September as the corpus's own 1997 coverage closes out.
